routine: My days have been much the same. I would rather keep this call brief.
I have kept to my usual schedule. Please do not put my name in a statement.
associates: I mostly spend time with people from work, but I will not speak for them.
That is a personal question. I do not think this line is private.
unusual: There has been talk, but I cannot separate what I saw from what I heard.
I noticed something out of place. I am not ready to say more over the telephone.
work: The office keeps its own records. You should look there.
I would prefer not to discuss my employer on this line.
worries: I am worried about being involved. Please do not call again.
Nothing I can say would help you. I am sorry.

routine: I keep a small timebook and mark each company bell; the order of a day helps me notice when something is out of place.
associates: I listen longer than I speak. People often tell me more once they have finished their first answer.
unusual: A detail can look ordinary until it appears twice. I have learned to keep the first copy.
work: I prefer to check the ledger before I answer for the office.
worries: I worry when a record is altered without a countersignature.

routine: I make the rounds, exchange a few courtesies, and keep the rest of my day to myself.
associates: I know plenty of names at the counter. Knowing a name is not the same as knowing a person.
unusual: There was a curious little interruption, though I would not care to repeat the story secondhand.
work: The company keeps excellent books. I let the proper desk speak for itself.
worries: Loose talk travels farther than a sealed letter.

routine: My schedule is written in the same pocket diary every week. I leave a margin for delays.
associates: I keep my acquaintances and my private correspondence in separate books.
unusual: I noted the date, but I cannot say what it meant.
work: I check the figures twice before the office seal goes on.
worries: A missing receipt causes more trouble than an honest mistake.

routine: Same tram, same bell, same queue at the company kiosk. There, that is the short version.
associates: If you want names, ask the directory. I have work to get back to.
unusual: I noticed it. I also noticed nobody wanted to file a report.
work: The figures are fine until a manager changes the form halfway through the shift.
worries: I worry about delays; every office charges somebody for them.

routine: I usually carry an extra ration chit for someone who missed the company counter.
associates: I help my neighbors, but I will not name them to a stranger on the wire.
unusual: I offered to help settle it. They were determined to manage alone.
work: I will cover a colleague's shift, but I still expect the rota to be corrected.
worries: People should not have to choose between a bill and a meal.

routine: I arrive early enough to read the notices before the senior clerks gather.
associates: I remember who attends each meeting. It is useful to know where decisions begin.
unusual: A sealed envelope changed hands after the office bell. I did not see its contents.
work: I am waiting for the next grade and keeping my evaluations in order.
worries: A careless signature can close doors for years.

routine: I take the quieter streets and notice which shop shutters are open on my way in.
associates: I spend time with a few people who do not ask me to raise my voice.
unusual: The room went quiet when one particular name was mentioned.
work: I do careful copying for the office; people forget the copyist can read.
worries: I worry when someone is being hurried into signing a form.

routine: I start with the morning notices, then someone at the kiosk always pulls me into a conversation.
associates: I know people from every floor, though I can never remember who introduced whom.
unusual: I meant to write it down, but the GATE announcement interrupted me.
work: I enjoy the company floor, even when I mislay the requisition slips.
worries: I keep forgetting to ask the registry about my delayed Credits.

routine: My route follows the delivery docket and the GATE bell schedule.
work: The dispatch office stamps each change to my route; I do not choose the addresses.

routine: I carry sealed packets between company counters and keep the receipt stubs in order.
work: A packet is delivered when the receiving desk signs for it. That is the whole of my authority.

routine: I reconcile the household and company ledgers before the evening bell.
work: Every transfer in my office needs a reference number and a second set of initials.

routine: I sort the morning forms before the public counter opens.
work: The company registry keeps duplicate copies; I only enter what is presented to me.

routine: I review the floor rota and the day's requisitions before staff arrive.
work: My authority ends at the company seal; matters beyond it go to the corporate office.

routine: I open the visitor book and check appointments against the office clock.
work: Visitors leave their company pass number at the desk, even when they say they are in a hurry.

routine: I prepare correspondence and the day's appointment cards before the first bell.
work: I keep carbon copies of signed instructions in the office file.

routine: I type the daily notices from approved copy and leave the original with the registry.
work: I can confirm a page was typed, but its author must answer for its contents.

routine: My day is measured in stops, stamped receipts, and the next GATE departure notice.
I follow the company bell, counter hours, and the printed rota.
I begin with the staff rota and finish by checking that the office seal is accounted for.
I set my own hours, though the company counters still close when their bell says so.
